meta.title: Who was the Mona Lisa? Facts and answers | Museum of Ages
meta.description: Who was the Mona Lisa? Lisa Gherardini of Florence, named in a note of 1503. Why it is so famous, the 1911 theft, where it hangs and what it is worth.
meta.og_title: Who was the Mona Lisa? Facts and answers
meta.og_image_alt: A reproduction of the Mona Lisa: a young woman in dark clothes sits half turned toward us, her hands resting one on the other, with hazy hills, water and a winding road far behind her.

top.answer: The woman in the Mona Lisa was Lisa Gherardini, who married Francesco del Giocondo, a silk merchant in Florence. The Louvre names her, and a note from October 1503 makes it firm: a clerk in Florence wrote that Leonardo was then painting Lisa del Giocondo's head. Leonardo da Vinci began the portrait around 1503 and kept working on it until he died in 1519. It hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

door.leads: This door takes you into the Leonardo wing, to her stop, “A woman called Lisa”.

blocks.answer: A Florentine woman, born in 1479 into an old family with land in the Chianti, who died in 1542. In 1495 she married Francesco del Giocondo, a silk merchant, and they had six children, the Louvre says.

pic.alt: A reproduction of the Mona Lisa: a young woman in dark clothes sits half turned toward us, her hands resting one on the other, with hazy hills, water and a winding road far behind her.

known: That she is the woman in the painting is firm: the Louvre names her, and it calls the doubts raised since the 20th century a false problem. The best evidence is a note written in October 1503 by Agostino Vespucci, a clerk in Florence, in a volume of Cicero's letters printed in 1477. Next to a passage about the ancient painter Apelles, who finished only the head and chest of a Venus, he wrote that Leonardo does the same in all his paintings, as in his head of Lisa del Giocondo.

Heidelberg University Library holds the book: a librarian came across the note there in 2005, and the university announced it in 2008. Her names are simple to explain: Mona is short for Madonna, my lady, and La Gioconda, in French La Joconde, is her husband's family name in its female form.
blocks.open: Little more is known about her life, the Louvre says, despite long searches in the archives. Vasari wrote in 1550 that her husband asked Leonardo to paint her, which the Louvre thinks may be so, and nobody knows whether she ever saw the portrait.
end: In our Leonardo wing she has a stop of her own,
, with a reproduction close to its real size.

blocks.h: Why is the Mona Lisa so famous?
blocks.answer: It was admired from the start, but a crime made it world famous, the Louvre says: the theft of 1911 spread its fame around the globe, above all among ordinary people.
known: The young Raphael learned from it, and in 1550 Giorgio Vasari praised it in his Lives of the Artists, though he had never seen it. It belonged to the French kings and went on show in the Louvre after the Revolution, yet it stayed one famous picture among many: between 1851 and 1880 copyists in the Louvre painted it 71 times, and a Murillo 197 times, the historian Donald Sassoon reports. In the same century writers such as Théophile Gautier and Walter Pater turned her into a beauty with a dangerous secret.

Then it vanished, in August 1911: crowds came to stare at the empty wall, and the news of its recovery in December 1913 made the front pages in France and America. Later it went on tour: in 1963 about 1.75 million people saw it in Washington and New York.
blocks.open: How much the theft alone did is still argued. Sassoon sees many causes adding up, from the kings' collection and the Louvre to the tours, mass tourism and advertising.

blocks.h: When was the Mona Lisa stolen?
blocks.answer: On 21 August 1911, from the Louvre. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian glazier who had worked at the museum, and the painting turned up in Florence in December 1913.
known: It was a Monday, when the Louvre was closed in those years, as the museum's own booklet on the theft tells it. The next day the painter Louis Béroud came to paint it and found it gone. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire spent a week in prison as a suspect, and Picasso was drawn in too, but neither was the thief.

Peruggia had worked for the firm that fitted protective glass to the Louvre's paintings, and he kept the panel with him in Paris for two years. In late 1913 he offered it to an art dealer in Florence, Alfredo Geri, who called in the director of the Uffizi, Giovanni Poggi. On 11 December the two inspected the panel at Peruggia's hotel, and on 12 December the police arrested him on the hotel stairs.

He said he had wanted to give back to Italy a painting stolen from it, but Leonardo had taken it to France himself. Italy showed it in Florence and Rome before it went back to Paris, and on 5 June 1914 a court in Florence sentenced Peruggia to a year and fifteen days.
blocks.open: How he got the panel out of the building we know only from his own later account. So the popular story that he hid overnight in a cupboard is not settled fact.

blocks.answer: In the Louvre in Paris, in the Salle des États, the largest room in the palace: Denon wing, level 1, room 711. It has hung in this room since 1966, apart from 1992 to 1995.

known: Since 2005 it has stood alone in the middle of the room, in a glass case that guards it and keeps temperature and humidity steady, because the poplar panel has warped and cracked. In 2019 the Louvre found that four in five of its visitors come to see it, and that they spend about 50 seconds looking at it. The Louvre is closed on Tuesdays, and
has the hours and the ticket prices.

Leonardo began it in Florence and brought it with him when he settled in France in 1516. You will often read 1503 to 1506 as its date, but the Louvre's own record says 1503 to 1519, because he kept painting it until he died and it was still unfinished then. It last left France in 1974, for Tokyo and Moscow, and since then it has stayed in the Louvre because it is so fragile.
blocks.open: It may move. In January 2025 France's president announced a room of its own with a separate way in, by 2031 at the latest, and in May 2026 the Louvre picked its architects but named no opening date.

blocks.h: How much is the Mona Lisa worth?
blocks.answer: Nobody can say, because it can never be sold. The figure you often read, 100 million US dollars, was an insurance valuation from 1962, and Guinness World Records still lists it as the highest ever for a painting.
known: That figure was set for the painting's trip to Washington and New York in 1962 and 1963. Guinness adds that the insurance was never taken out, because the tightest security cost less than the premiums would have.

The painting belongs to the French state, and French law, article L. 451-5 of the Code du patrimoine, makes museum collections owned by public bodies inalienable: they cannot be sold or given away. Long before the record, an estimate of 1849 put it at 90,000 francs, below several paintings by Raphael. Today it is not insured at all, Guinness wrote in 2026.
blocks.open: It has not been sold since the French king bought it, so it has no market price. Even Guinness, which keeps the 1962 record, says the painting has never been valued.

blocks.h: Is the Mona Lisa in the Louvre the real one?
blocks.answer: Yes. The painting behind the glass is Leonardo's original, and the Louvre follows its path from his hands to the French kings and into the museum.
known: When it turned up in 1913, the Uffizi's director, Giovanni Poggi, examined the panel and declared it Leonardo's. More than a hundred old copies are known, the Louvre says.

A foundation in Zurich claims that another picture, the Isleworth Mona Lisa, is an earlier version by Leonardo. Leading experts reject it: the Leonardo scholar Martin Kemp points out that it is on canvas, and Leonardo is not known to have painted on canvas.

paras: The Prado in Madrid holds a copy that was painted in Leonardo's own workshop, beside the original as experts think, and both museums accept it as the earliest known copy. In 2011 and 2012 restorers took a later black overpaint off it and found the scenery behind her. Its colours are far brighter than those of the original, which lies under yellowed varnish.

blocks.open: Who painted the Prado copy is not known: Leonardo's pupils Salaì and Melzi have been named, and other experts doubt both. Where the Isleworth picture was before 1913 is unknown, even by the foundation's own account.
end: The Mona Lisa among his other works, with how sure each one is his:

blocks.intro: Some things people say about the painting are claims, and some are myths. Each is marked as what it is, with what good sources say.

items.name: A hidden secret
items.claim: A popular claim: the painting hides a secret.
items.known: The Louvre calls that an absurd myth, born of 19th-century writers' fantasies. Her husband's name, Giocondo, means happy in Italian, and the Louvre suggests the smile may play on it.

items.name: Letters hidden in her eyes
items.claim: In 2010 the Italian researcher Silvano Vinceti claimed that tiny letters are hidden in her eyes, LV in the right one.
items.known: It remains a claim. The Louvre's own text on the painting counts hidden secrets as a myth.

items.name: She is Leonardo himself
items.claim: In 1987 the computer artist Lillian Schwartz claimed the face is partly Leonardo's own, after matching it on screen with a mirrored drawing thought to be his self-portrait.
items.known: Even her own collaborator did not think this proved anything, and art historians were sceptical. The note of 1503 names the sitter: Lisa.

items.name: Her eyes follow you
items.claim: Her eyes follow you around the room, people say.
items.known: That effect is real for portraits that look straight out, but not for her. In a 2019 study at Bielefeld University, viewers saw her gaze turned about 15 degrees to their right on average, too far off to feel looked at.

items.name: Her missing eyebrows
items.claim: She once had eyebrows: in 2007 the engineer Pascal Cotte claimed that his high-resolution scans showed a trace of the left one.
items.known: Today she has no visible eyebrows or lashes. Vasari praised her eyebrows in 1550, but he never saw the painting, so nobody knows for sure.

items.name: Napoleon took it from Italy
items.claim: A claim the thief of 1911 believed: Napoleon stole the painting from Italy.
items.known: No. It came to France with Leonardo in 1516, long before Napoleon, and in 1518 the French king very probably paid for it. Napoleon only kept it in his bedroom for a while, the historian Donald Sassoon writes.
